120.subtitle: Sun in the heart, lamp in the triangle, Dakṣa's ruined rite

commentary.meaning: The first line completes the descent begun in the previous verse. She was at the crown with the colour of the moon and at the brow with the colours of a rainbow; now she is in the heart and she is like the sun, and the change from cool light to burning light is the point of the arrangement. The third name then does something unexpected: instead of moving to a fourth place in the body it moves into the diagram, calling her the lamp inside the triangle, which is the innermost figure of the Śrīcakra. Body and diagram are being treated as the same interior. The second line breaks off entirely and turns to mythology, giving three names in a row that begin with the same syllable and tell one story between them. She is Dakṣa's daughter; she is the killer of demons; she is the destroyer of Dakṣa's sacrifice. The verse ends on the six-hundredth name, and it ends with a rite deliberately wrecked by the deity in whose honour rites are performed.
commentary.history:
Hṛdayasthā continues the sequence of placements. The heart in Sanskrit anatomy is not primarily the organ of feeling that English usage makes it: hṛdaya is where the self is said to dwell in the Upaniṣads, the cavity described as smaller than a grain of rice and larger than the worlds, and the seat of knowing as much as of emotion. To place her there after the crown and the brow is to move from the top of the head, through the point between the eyes, to the traditional dwelling of the ātman. The light changes accordingly: raviprakhyā, looking like the sun, replaces the moon of two names earlier. The pairing of a lunar crown with a solar heart belongs to a widespread set of correlations in which the two luminaries are distributed through the body, the moon storing nectar above and the sun consuming it below.

Trikoṇāntaradīpikā leaves the body without announcing that it is doing so. The trikoṇa is the central triangle of the Śrīcakra, the innermost of the nine interlocking figures, and it is the enclosure in which the bindu, the single point at the centre, is set. Dīpikā is a small lamp, the ordinary oil lamp of a household shrine, and it is also the standard title for a commentary — the thing that illuminates a text. She is the flame inside the triangle: not the triangle, not the point, but what makes them visible. Set immediately after three placements in the body, the name asserts an identification that the tradition makes everywhere and argues for nowhere in particular — that the diagram drawn on metal and the interior of the practitioner are one place described twice.

The second line turns to the oldest and most consequential story in Śaiva mythology. Dakṣa was a patriarch, one of the progenitors of creatures, and his daughter Satī married Śiva against his wishes; Dakṣa regarded his son-in-law as an unwashed outsider with bad companions. He then performed a great sacrifice and invited every divinity except Śiva. Satī went uninvited, was insulted by her father, and destroyed herself — in most tellings by yogic fire generated within her own body, which is the origin of her name as it came to be used. Śiva, told of it, tore a lock of his hair and produced Vīrabhadra, who led the host that broke up the sacrifice, scattered the gods, and beheaded Dakṣa; the head was afterwards replaced with a goat's. Satī is then reborn as Pārvatī, daughter of the mountain, and marries Śiva again. In a further development, Śiva carries her corpse across the world in grief until it is cut apart, and the places where the pieces fall become the śākta pīṭhas, the seats of the goddess, which is how the story ends up underwriting the sacred geography of the entire tradition.

Dākṣāyaṇī is a patronymic, a feminine formed directly from Dakṣa, and it is not a compound; the module's note is right to flag this, since the surrounding names are almost all compounds and the ear expects one here. Dakṣayajñavināśinī then names the outcome. It is worth being clear about who does what. In the Purāṇic narratives the destruction of the sacrifice is carried out by Vīrabhadra and Śiva's host, not by the goddess directly, and the hymn's attribution of it to her is a deliberate shift of agency — the kind of shift Śākta texts make routinely when they take over material composed from a Śaiva point of view. Some traditions soften this by reading the name as she who is the cause of the destruction; others take it at face value. The reading is not settled, and the disagreement is itself part of the history of the name.

Daityahantrī, between the two, widens the frame. Daityas are the sons of Diti, the antigods of Purāṇic cosmology, and the epithet slayer of Daityas belongs to the goddess of the Devī Māhātmya more than to Satī. Its placement here folds the whole martial career of the goddess into the Dakṣa story, so that the ruin of the sacrifice appears as one instance of a general pattern rather than as a family quarrel. Note also the sound: dākṣāyaṇī, daityahantrī, dakṣayajñavināśinī, three names in a row on the same syllable, closing the line and the six hundredth name together.
commentary.practice:
The first line gives you the vocalic ṛ again, at the very start of hṛdayasthā, and immediately after an aspirated h. Say the h with breath, then the ṛ as a full short vowel with the tongue curled, then da and ya, then the sthā cluster with its dental s and aspirated dental th. Four distinct movements in four syllables.

Raviprakhyā ends in khyā, an aspirated guttural kh followed by the palatal glide y. It is a cluster that rewards slowing down, because the aspiration has to be audible before the y begins; kh-y-ā, not ky-ā. Trikoṇāntaradīpikā is eight syllables and holds the third quarter of the verse by itself. Its ṇ is retroflex, and it is retroflex because of the r in tri three syllables earlier — the same rule that gives sākṣiṇī and mṛṇāla their ṇ, operating here across an unusually long distance. The joint in the middle of the word is worth seeing: trikoṇa plus antara gives trikoṇāntara, because a short a followed by a short a yields a single long ā.

The second line is the easiest in this group to say and the easiest to garble, because all three names begin with d and two of them contain kṣ. Fix them by length: four syllables, four syllables, eight. Dākṣāyaṇī has a long ā in both of its first two syllables and a retroflex ṇ; dakṣa in the last name has short a. That contrast between dākṣā and dakṣa is the difference between the patronymic and the father's own name, and getting it wrong is a grammatical error, not merely a mispronunciation. Daityahantrī opens with the diphthong ai, a full long vowel, and closes with the ntrī cluster already met in niyantrī. In dakṣayajñavināśinī the jña conjunct appears again — follow whatever convention your teacher uses — and the ś is the palatal sibilant, distinct from the retroflex ṣ two syllables before it.

For the archanā: hṛdayasthāyai, raviprakhyāyai, trikoṇāntaradīpikāyai, dākṣāyaṇyai, daityahantryai, dakṣayajñavināśinyai. The first three are ā-stems and take -āyai; the last three are ī-stems and contract to -yai. The verse thus divides cleanly by declension along the same line where it divides by subject, which makes it easy to hold in the memory.

This is also the verse that completes the six hundredth name, and reciters who keep count will mark it. What it asks is a tolerance for two difficulties at once. The first line requires holding an interior image — a sun in the chest, a flame inside a triangle — and the discipline there is not to hurry, since eight syllables of name give ample time to see something. The second line requires something else. It is a story about a father who would not invite his daughter's husband, a daughter who died of it, and a sacrifice torn apart in revenge, and it is being recited as praise. The tradition does not offer a resolution of that, and it is better not to invent one. The plainest way to take the verse is that the deity being addressed is not on the side of ritual as such, that she has broken up a rite before and may do so again, and that the person performing one in front of her is not thereby in a position of safety.

crossReferences.translation: Now, there is this city of brahman, and in it a dwelling, a small lotus, and within that a small space. What is inside that is what should be sought out; that, certainly, is what one should desire to know.
crossReferences.relevance: The passage that establishes the heart as a place with an inside. The city of brahman is the body, the small lotus is the heart, and the text's whole procedure is to send the seeker inwards to a space of no measurable size and then to say that this space is as wide as the sky. Hṛdayasthā depends on that background, and so does the move made two names later, when an interior that has just been located in the chest is relocated inside a drawn triangle.

crossReferences.deva: ईश्वरः सर्वभूतानां हृद्देशेऽर्जुन तिष्ठति । भ्रामयन्सर्वभूतानि यन्त्रारूढानि मायया ॥
crossReferences.iast: īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ hṛddeśe 'rjuna tiṣṭhati | bhrāmayan sarvabhūtāni yantrārūḍhāni māyayā ||
crossReferences.translation: The lord stands in the region of the heart of all beings, Arjuna, whirling them round by his power of appearance as though they were mounted on a machine.
crossReferences.relevance: The most familiar statement in Sanskrit of the doctrine that hṛdayasthā compresses into four syllables, and a useful corrective to reading the name sentimentally. The verse pairs the heart-dwelling with the word yantra in its ordinary mechanical sense, a device on which things are made to turn — which is the same word that this tradition uses for the diagram in whose triangle the next name places her.

references.title: Classical Hindu Mythology: A Reader in the Sanskrit Purāṇas
references.author: Cornelia Dimmitt and J. A. B. van Buitenen (Temple University Press, 1978)
references.note: Contains translated Purāṇic accounts of the destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice, which is the fastest way to see how much the tellings differ from one another — who insults whom, how Satī dies, and how much of the violence is attributed to Śiva, to Vīrabhadra, or to the goddess herself. Read two versions before deciding what the last name of this verse is claiming.

references.title: Hindu Goddesses: Visions of the Divine Feminine in the Hindu Religious Tradition
references.author: David R. Kinsley (University of California Press, 1986)
references.note: Good on Satī and on the pīṭhas — the network of shrines said to mark where the pieces of her body fell — which is the part of the Dakṣa story that turned a myth into a map. Also useful for seeing how the figure of Satī was gradually absorbed into the larger goddess of the Śākta traditions.

references.title: Auspicious Wisdom: The Texts and Traditions of Śrīvidyā Śākta Tantrism in South India
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (SUNY Press, 1992)
references.note: For the central triangle. Brooks works through the construction of the Śrīcakra and the nine enclosures, so that trikoṇāntaradīpikā stops being a phrase and becomes a location you could point to on a plate. The discussion of the bindu is what makes sense of calling her a lamp rather than the figure itself.

references.title: The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation
references.author: Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 1998)
references.note: For the heart. Chāndogya 8.1 is quoted above; read it alongside the passages in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka that place the self in the heart, and the compressed statement of the name hṛdayasthā will unfold into a doctrine with several centuries of argument behind it.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Useful here for dakṣa, where the entry gives the adjective sense — able, competent, dexterous — before the proper name, and for dīpikā, where the range runs from a small lamp to the title of an explanatory commentary. Both senses are live in this verse.
